articles.title: In 2018, Matt Holliday paid $3 million for Oklahoma land; years later, his 62-acre estate with a baseball field and $2 million pool is asking $9.8 million
articles.summary: US News: A private baseball field, professional lighting, batting cages, an indoor sports court and a swimming pool reportedly worth about $2 million are among.
articles.body: A private baseball field, professional lighting, batting cages, an indoor sports court and a swimming pool reportedly worth about $2 million are among the features of a sprawling Oklahoma estate built by former Major League Baseball star Matt Holliday. Located at 3003 S Country Club Road in Stillwater, the property was created as a family home and training ground after Holliday purchased the land in 2018. According to the current listing by Wyatt Poindexter, the 62-acre estate is now asking $9.8 million, after initially entering the market for $12 million in February 2026. The home was built in 2022 and spans 7,500 square feet, with five bedrooms, seven bathrooms and a long list of indoor and outdoor amenities.A Stillwater property with a baseball connectionHolliday, who was born and raised in Stillwater, built the property after purchasing the land for about $3 million in 2018. He and his wife, Leslee, completed construction of the main residence in 2022. The home was designed as a one-level estate inspired by Texas Hill Country architecture. Its exterior combines stone and metal roofing, while oversized windows bring natural light into the main living spaces.Inside, the 7,500-square-foot residence has an open-plan living area incorporating the kitchen, dining and lounge spaces. There is also a butler's pantry, two offices and five bedrooms. The primary suite includes two closets, while the layout is designed around both family life and entertaining. The property is currently being offered with around $3 million worth of custom furniture included, according to the listing. The home's baseball memorabilia, however, is not part of the sale.A baseball field built for the familyThe most distinctive feature of the estate is outside the house. The property includes a full-size baseball field with professional turf, stadium-style lighting and seating. There are also batting cages and a large fire pit positioned behind home plate. The field was built with Holliday's sons in mind. His eldest son, Jackson Holliday, was selected first overall by the Baltimore Orioles in the 2022 MLB Draft and made his major-league debut in 2024. Ethan Holliday was selected fourth overall by the Colorado Rockies in the 2025 MLB Draft.The listing agent, Wyatt Poindexter, told Realtor.com that Holliday essentially used the property as a place to train his sons. The baseball facilities therefore form a particularly personal part of the estate rather than simply being decorative luxury amenities.More than a baseball compoundAlthough baseball is the property's defining feature, the estate has been designed around a much broader collection of recreational and entertainment spaces. The grounds include a putting green, running trails, a pond, a guest house and a workshop. There is also a gym and an indoor court that accommodates both basketball and pickleball. The outdoor area includes a hot tub and an outdoor kitchen, providing additional spaces for entertaining.Another major feature is the two-level swimming pool. According to Realtor.com, the pool includes a waterfall, a swim-through grotto and built-in seating areas. The listing agent estimated its cost at approximately $2 million. Together, the amenities make the property less like a conventional luxury residence and more like a private sports and recreation compound.Designed for gatheringsHolliday has also described the home in terms of the people who have spent time there. In a statement reported by Realtor.com, he said one of the things he valued most about the property was its ability to bring people together. He recalled hosting college students and professional athletes for meals, conversations and fellowship. That emphasis is reflected in the home's design. The open-plan living space connects the kitchen, dining and lounge areas, while the large grounds provide numerous spaces for outdoor activities and gatherings. The estate is also being sold furnished, apart from Holliday's baseball memorabilia.From a $12 million launch to a $9.8 million asking priceWhen the property first came to market in February 2026, it was listed for $12 million. At that time, Realtor.com reported that the price made it the most expensive single-family home listed in Oklahoma. The current listing, however, shows the asking price at $9.8 million, reflecting a $2.2 million reduction from the original price. The listing remains active, with the property described as a 62-acre estate and the residence measuring 7,500 square feet. The property sits about 40 minutes from Edmond, according to the current listing, while Stillwater is Holliday's hometown.A home shaped by Holliday's baseball legacyHolliday spent 15 seasons in Major League Baseball, playing for the Colorado Rockies, Oakland Athletics, St. Louis Cardinals and New York Yankees. He was a seven-time All-Star and won the World Series with the Cardinals in 2011. His Oklahoma estate reflects that career in an unusually direct way. Rather than simply displaying baseball memorabilia, the property incorporates the sport into its physical design through a dedicated field, batting cages and training facilities.Now on the market, the estate offers a future owner something considerably different from a standard luxury home: a 7,500-square-foot residence set across 62 acres, with a private baseball field, indoor sports facilities, extensive outdoor amenities and a pool that alone was estimated at $2 million. For Holliday, the property was built around family, baseball and bringing people together. For its next owner, it is now a high-end Oklahoma estate with a very distinctive piece of sports history built into the grounds.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'My rent was higher than my student loan' - the booming cost of private halls
articles.summary: Private student halls are springing up in Scotland's cities in ever increasing numbers yet rents continue to soar.
articles.body:
You don't have to walk far in any university city before spotting some form of private Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA).

These large blocks of student housing are springing up in cities across the UK, yet rents continue to soar and young people studying at university say they're still finding it difficult to secure a place to live.

The increase in PBSA has predominantly been driven by private companies, with many developments targeting more affluent international and postgraduate students, who industry experts say are becoming increasingly important to the sector.

Developers say they are meeting a market demand but campaigners argue that they are too expensive for most Scottish students and more affordable housing should be being built instead.

Twenty-year-old Lara Reader told the BBC that when she applied for student accommodation at Edinburgh University she did not expect to be allocated the most expensive option on her list.

Like many first-year students, Lara selected from a mix of university-owned and privately-operated halls which cater solely to the city's huge student population.

She was given a room in Brae House, one of the many private PBSAs in the city.

PBSAs typically offer en-suite bedrooms and studio apartments alongside premium facilities such as gyms, study areas and social spaces - but they also come at a higher price point than traditional student halls.

The rent for Lara's room was £1,022 per month, more than £200 higher than her monthly student maintenance loan.

Despite it being beyond her budget, Lara accepted the offer because of the difficulty of finding student housing in Edinburgh.

She said the cost hung over much of her first year at university and she was "constantly stressing" about how much money she was having to put towards rent.

To cover the shortfall, she worked 20 hours per week alongside her studies, a decision she says contributed to her failing her first-year exams.

"I was exhausted all the time," she said. "I just didn't have enough time to study."

"I think when pricing student housing they need to be more realistic.

"It makes it so difficult for students like me who don't come from a super wealthy background to find an affordable place to live."

The University of Edinburgh said it offered students good value, across a broad range of price points, with entry-level rents being well below the average.

A spokesperson said: "We encourage students to select accommodation that aligns with their lifestyle preferences and budget throughout the application process."

How much purpose-built student accommodation is there?

Across the UK, a total of 206,005 students told the Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) they lived in private-sector halls in 2024/25.

This is up from 117,995 a decade earlier.

The rate of increase is higher in Scotland, up from 5,500 in 2014/15 to 14,640 last year.

The growth of PBSA has been particularly visible in Scotland's two largest cities.

As of August 2026, Glasgow has 21,655 student beds with a further 18,213 in the development pipeline, meaning the city could host almost 40,000 student beds if all proposed schemes go ahead.

Edinburgh has also seen rapid growth, with the supply of PBSA increasing by almost 60% over the past decade.

A further 5,917 beds were in the development pipeline as of December 2025.

Richard Ward, the head of research at student accommodation marketing website StuRents, said the average cost of privately-operated PBSA in Edinburgh and Glasgow is £268 and £243 per person per week (pppw) respectively.

The national average (excluding London) is £191pppw.

He said: "The rents you're having to charge are about £250 to £300 per week to make a scheme financially viable

"The challenge for the sector is, at that price point, a lot of domestic students cannot afford that."

According to industry experts, international students, who are often better able to afford higher rents, are a key part of the PBSA market.

It's something Lara, from Kelso in the Borders, noticed in her accommodation too.

"A lot of people I was friends with through my accommodation were international students, so funding is very different," she said.

"I think for the most part, a lot of people didn't have as much of a struggle paying the rent, but I definitely know a few people who were in the same boat as I was."

For many international students, however, PBSA offers reassurance that can be difficult to find in the private rental market.

Saba, an international student from Pakistan who had planned to study in Glasgow, said they felt safer than trying to organise a flat from the other side of the world.

"I didn't really know where to start," she said. "Every country has different laws when it comes to properties and renting places."

After missing out on university accommodation, she considered trying to find a property through a private landlord, however, she says she "encountered a bunch of scammers" during her search, including one man who asked for £500 upfront before sending videos of the property.

"As an international student, I feel like you're vulnerable" she said

"There are good and bad people everywhere and the bad lot try to take advantage of that."

John Boyle, director of research and strategy at estate agency Rettie, said purpose-built student accommodation had become one of the most "financially viable" forms of city-centre development, with developers often able to achieve higher returns than from conventional residential schemes, making projects easier to fund and deliver.

"The reason the buildings are going up is because other buildings have gone up and have been successful," he said.

He added that high land values and development costs meant schemes such as affordable housing are often difficult to deliver in prime locations.

Developers also argue that PBSA helps meet demand from growing student populations while reducing pressure on the wider rental market.

Edinburgh and Glasgow city councils both declared formal housing emergencies in 2023.

Campaigners argue the rapid expansion of PBSA is not addressing the housing challenges faced by many students and residents.

Aditi Jehangir, secretary of Living Rent Edinburgh, said: "Scotland does not need more unaffordable, poor-quality purpose-built student accommodation.

"Purpose-built student accommodation is completely unaffordable and not the answer to the housing crisis.

"Throughout Scotland's cities, we have seen development after development spring up, taking up space that could be used for much-needed social housing."

She added that PBSA was "extremely lucrative to developers", did little to meet the needs of local communities and that many units remained empty.

Data from StuRents suggests occupancy rates have fallen in both Edinburgh and Glasgow.

According to figures from June 2026, about 49.7% of rooms in Glasgow had been booked for the upcoming academic year, in comparison to 81.8% of rooms at the same point in 2024.

Similarly, Edinburgh figures suggest that 63.2% of rooms have been booked in the same period, down from 80.6% in 2024.

Nationally, 59.1% of rooms had been booked for the upcoming year in June 2026, compared with 70.4% in 2024.

StuRents' Richard Ward added that the sector had experienced a surge in demand from international and postgraduate students following the Covid pandemic.

However, he said growth in international student numbers had slowed, while new accommodation continued to come onto the market, leading to lower occupancy rates.

International student figures in Scotland have fallen for two years in a row, with a 5% drop most recently.

The largest cohort of international students in Scotland come from China.

Ward said: "The challenge for developers and investors entering into the student market is that from the point of an application being approved to the building actually being complete could be three years, for example.

"During that time the local market could have radically shifted."

Because of this, Ward says that pipeline figures do not necessarily translate into completed developments.

"I'm not expecting, by all means, anywhere near the full pipeline to be delivered in any market, but equally in Glasgow and Edinburgh," he said.

articles.title: Plaid warned not to cut help for poorer children if it wants Labour to back budget
articles.summary: Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates makes early years programme Flying Start a red line in negotiations.
articles.body:
Welsh Labour has said it will not support the Welsh government's budget if cuts are made to a flagship early years programme.

The party's leader, Ken Skates, said the future of the Flying Start scheme "has to be a red line" in his party's ongoing budget talks with the government.

A Plaid Cymru government minister praised aspects of the scheme but did not say whether it would continue in its current form.

The Welsh government said support for "disadvantaged children will be enhanced" as it expands its free childcare policy.

Plaid Cymru is running the Welsh government without a majority of seats in the Senedd , meaning that it has to strike deals with other political parties in Cardiff Bay in order to pass budgets or new laws.

First launched in 2007, the Flying Start scheme was primarily designed to help children in the poorer areas of the country with their language, social and physical development before starting school.

It also includes 12.5 hours of free childcare for two-year-olds, and is being expanded Wales-wide as part of the Welsh government's ultimate policy aim of providing free childcare 20 hours a week to all children between nine months and four years.

£55m to boost childcare for two-year-olds, Welsh government says

Plan to expand free childcare in Wales faces serious challenges, figures show

Since May's election, the new government has been under pressure to explain how it was going to fund its flagship childcare policy.

The Welsh government's latest estimate is that it would require between £250m and £500m of extra funding a year, depending on how many parents make use of the scheme.

Speaking at an event held by the Senedd Sources podcast on Tuesday, Plaid's Minister for Government Effectiveness, Dafydd Trystan Davies, did not rule out cutting or changing the Flying Start programme.

Asked if he could guarantee that the scheme would still be available by the time of the next Senedd election, he replied: "I don't think I can guarantee that any single programme will be in its current form."

Davies said: "What is really strong and important with Flying Start is those areas around speech and language therapy, is around the health aspect.

"So, can you guarantee that those provisions of Flying Start will be there as part of the [childcare] offer? Clearly, it has to be.

"What I've seen with Flying Start is the budget allocated to different councils. Some councils have been far more effective at delivering to a large number of poor and disadvantaged children and therefore, what I'm keen to see there, is that all councils adopt the best practice.

"As has been done in various contexts, you can target that provision."

Back in July, the government lost a Senedd vote on extra spending plans after failing to strike a deal with Welsh Labour.

Plaid and Welsh Labour are currently holding fresh budget negotiations around this year's supplementary budget and next year's full budget.

In an interview with BBC Walescast , Welsh Labour Leader Ken Skates said: "It appears they're looking at using Flying Start money to pay for something they never costed during the election or in their manifesto, the childcare offer, which will benefit a lot of middle class and upper class families.

"But it's going to be people and children who benefit from Flying Start who will pay the price.

"I would be deeply disappointed if Plaid didn't commit to the future of Flying Start."

Asked if any change to Flying Start would rule his party out of supporting the budget, Skates replied: "For us as a party, I think it has to be a red line.

"If Plaid Cymru think they can take the best of Flying Start and apply it in different areas, I'm afraid they're going to let people down badly.

"So, I'm afraid, if they're talking about Flying Start, then they're going to have to do it by themselves, without our consent or support and they won't be getting a budget approval from us."

Steffan Evans, head of the Bevan Foundation, said: "The majority of children living in poverty are not in Flying Start areas.

"So, if we want to get a childcare system that helps child development in terms of the education and parents back into work and gets to those children in poverty, you do have to strike a compromise, I think, in terms of how that operates.

"And that might mean going towards something more universal to get to more children, rather than something that's perfect, but only answers part of the problem."

Reform's minister for fairness, families and communities, Cristiana Emsley, said: "Plaid Cymru are raising the prospect of cutting funding for vulnerable children while continuing to spend money on overseas embassies, its Nation of Sanctuary programme and tree planting in Uganda.

"At a time when families across Wales are struggling with the cost of living and children are in need of support, it is clear Plaid have the wrong priorities."

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "Our offer means that childcare will be more accessible and affordable to all families.

"The current phase of delivery which will provide funded childcare for all two-year-olds is being delivered through the Flying Start model.

"At the same time, the support available to disadvantaged children will be enhanced as a result of our offer.

"We will need to substantially increase the number of providers to ensure that families have childcare options that work for them.

"These are all matters under discussion by the Expert Group on Childcare as we work on rolling out the next phase of this ambitious policy."

articles.title: Dramatic recording could help answer why NBC4 helicopter crashed
articles.summary: At a news conference Wednesday, federal transportation officials said the most critical information available so far has been video captured from the helicop...
articles.body:
It was a night of devastation in Chatsworth that began with a deadly Metro bus collision and ended with the fiery crash of an NBC4 helicopter covering the news that left two journalists and, on the ground, a bystander dead.

Tuesday's scene was a mixture of confusion and chaos, with first responders fanned out across two catastrophes and television news teams desperately trying to find out whether their journalists were safe. The crashes claimed the lives of five people and left others with various degrees of injury.

Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration were trying Wednesday to determine exactly what caused the news helicopter, a Eurocopter AS350 B2, to go down.

NTSB Investigator Fabian Salazar said officials are searching through the wreckage, combing through maintenance logbooks, security footage, weather reports and witness interviews, and reviewing the pilot's training to figure out what went wrong.

But the most critical information so far has been audio captured from the helicopter during a live broadcast of reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw's final moments before it crashed.

The footage shows an aerial view of the bus crash with the whirl of the helicopter in the background. Suddenly, the sound of the engine's motor winds down and a horn blares, possibly warning the pilot that the main rotor speed had dropped too low or the helicopter had lost hydraulics. Moreno responds to the noise with a quiet "uh oh."

The angle of the camera begins to descend and Moreno is heard asking "You can't pull up?" before the video cuts out. Moreno, Marciniw and 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, who was on the ground when the chopper went down around 7 p.m., were killed.

"That video is probably the most important piece of evidence we have recovered so far," Salazar said.

Aviation experts told The Times the crash might be the result of a mechanical failure with the 22-year-old aircraft, a common helicopter for news and law enforcement organizations because of its general reliability.

Zoey Tur, a veteran news helicopter pilot who operated the type of helicopter the NBC4 crew was flying, said the sound the microphone picked up was of the engine shutting down.

"First, the engine starts winding down, which in turn reduces power to the rotor blades. Then you hear the horn warning of low rotor RPM. You can even hear the blade slap slow down," Tur said.

But, Tur pointed out, the fire that resulted when the copter crashed indicated there was still fuel onboard, so the engines likely shut down for another reason.

When a helicopter's rotors stop rotating, there's a safety maneuver known as autorotation where the pilot can try to gain enough momentum and upward flow on the rotor blades to increase their rotation, which helps control the aircraft as it descends, said Jack Cress, a former helicopter pilot for the U.S. Marine Corps and a helicopter accident investigation instructor at USC's Aviation Safety and Security Program.

Cress compared the maneuver to a fixed-wing airplane gliding through the air with the force generated by its wings but, in this case, the helicopter would use the upward force on its rotors caused by descending, or moving forward, to make the rotors turn fast enough to keep the craft in relative control.

But Cress said the fact that the helicopter appeared to be hovering in the air, and at a low altitude, would make it difficult for the pilot to execute the maneuver.

"In this case, he's in the worst part of the height-velocity curve," Cress said, referring to a chart used by helicopter pilots that tracks height and air speed for safe flight conditions. "That is a dangerous place to be."

Helicopter pilots are trained to stay away from those conditions, Cress said, because the lack of altitude and forward momentum give pilots little recourse if there is engine trouble. But for news helicopters and police choppers, hovering and maintaining low altitude is a common practice, he said.

Those conditions of hovering in the air, with little altitude and no momentum, are commonly referred to by helicopter pilots as a "dead man's curve," said Jeff Guzzetti, a former NTSB and FAA investigator who is also an instructor with USC's Aviation Safety and Security Program.

"That's the worst place to be if you have a problem," Guzzetti said.

The helicopter was owned by Tiny Bubbles Aviation Inc., a holding company with a business address listed at Whiteman Airport in Pacoima, according to state and FAA records. The company is listed as the owner of at least six aircraft, including five helicopters.

Lawrence Welk, who is listed in public records as an agent of Tiny Bubbles Aviation, is also president of Welk Aviation, a company that according to its website owns and operates news helicopters for KNBC and KTLA.

In a brief phone call on Wednesday, Welk confirmed to The Times that the company was working with investigators, but declined to comment on the incident.

"I just got back from the accident scene," Welk said.

The bus crash brought an army of first responders and news media to the area, including TV news choppers flying overhead. Residents gathered around the bus to figure out what was going on.

Then, everyone heard an explosion and saw a fireball rising a few blocks away. Many ran to that scene, where a fire was raging. Firefighters tried to battle the blaze while police pushed back the public and reporters. There were rumors immediately that a news chopper had crashed.

NBC4 anchor Colleen Williams told viewers the station had lost contact with its chopper crew. Around 9 p.m., she confirmed the NBC4 team had crashed.

The helicopter went down between two commercial buildings in the 9100 block of Mason Avenue, smashing into a pair of truck cargo containers.

The situation thrust the team at NBC4 into a journalist's nightmare — a tragedy where reporters become part of the story.

"They were sacrificing their lives in service of their community," NBC morning anchor Lynette Romero told viewers, with her co-anchors by her side. "They were determined and dedicated until the very end doing the job they loved so much. Our hearts are heavy this morning but we are here with you, we are here for you as we try to navigate these tragedies together."

On Wednesday, authorities announced they had arrested Bailee Lynn Rios, who they said was driving the SUV that slammed into the bus, on suspicion of murder.

Rios, 36, is being held in lieu of $4 million bail, according to jail records.

Los Angeles police said Rios was driving a gray 2004 Ford Expedition around 5 p.m. Tuesday southbound in the northbound lanes on De Soto Avenue when she ran a red light at Nordhoff Street. The SUV narrowly avoided a car driving through the intersection before crashing into the side of the Metro Line 166 bus.

The violent crash ejected one passenger from the bus and partially ejected a second person, according to police. Two passengers, identified as 31-year-old Gage Weida and 46-year-old Daniel Castillo of Arleta, died at the scene.

One passenger, who suffered severe injuries, and five others with non-life-threatening injures were taken to hospitals.

The chain of events left residents shaken. "Anybody could be gone in a minute, you know?" Winnetka resident Michael Sanchez, a physical therapist, said.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Women sue Epstein’s estate, saying their photos were found in his vast child porn collection
articles.summary: The lawsuit alleges Epstein kept a “modeling book” containing “sexualized images of children” in a locked safe.
articles.body: Two women filed a federal lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s estate, claiming their photographs were found in his vast collection of child pornography. Identified in court papers only as Jane Doe and Amy, the women allege that “few if any” of those whose photos were in Epstein’s collection were informed that these photographs are in the hands of federal investigators. The lawsuit, filed Tuesday in the Southern District of New York, seeks class-action status and is asking for unspecified damages and requesting the court to “design and supervise a single, coordinated program for identifying and notifying” the other women whose “unlawful sexualized images” were part of Epstein’s collection. “One of Epstein’s most horrific but often overlooked crimes was his possession, transportation, production, and distribution of child pornography and/or child sexual abuse material (together ‘CSAM’) of countless children,” the lawsuit says. “Beginning in the early 1990s until his death in 2019, Epstein, along with his co-conspirators, created and participated in a multi-decade, vast CSAM conspiracy,” it says. The lawsuit alleges that Epstein kept a “modeling book” containing “sexualized images of children” in a locked safe. No CSAM charges were filed against Epstein, and according to the lawsuit, Epstein and unnamed co-conspirators alleged the images “were for the purposes of developing child models for Victoria’s Secret.” “This lawsuit holds Jeffrey Epstein’s estate accountable for a crime that has never been fully addressed on its own terms,” one of the accusers’ lawyers, Hillary Nappi of AWK Survivor Advocate Attorneys, said in an emailed response to questions. Named as defendants in their capacities as co-executors of Epstein’s estate are his longtime lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn. Their lawyer, Daniel Weiner, declined to comment. Epstein died by suicide in 2019 at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City, where he was jailed while he was awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. Allegations that Epstein and co-conspirators “created what they referred to as a ‘modeling book’” were previously mentioned in a lawsuit Epstein survivor Maria Farmer filed against the government. Her case alleges that the government failed to protect her and others from Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. “Although they claimed that the ‘book’ was for the purposes of developing child models for Victoria’s Secret, the book contained nude or partially nude sexualized images of children,” the lawsuit filed Tuesday says. Jane Doe says in the lawsuit that she was around 12 years old when “Epstein stole partially nude photographs of her” that were “taken as part of an artist study.” “In Epstein’s possession and given the manner in which he obtained, catalogued, and retained them alongside a collection of sexualized images of children, the Jane Doe Images constituted a lascivious exhibition” that Epstein took with him across state lines, the lawsuit says. “Despite contemporaneous reports made to law enforcement, specifically alerting law enforcement that Epstein had obtained these photos of Jane Doe, and similar photos of another minor, no one in law enforcement took action to prosecute anyone or even investigate these reports,” it says. Meanwhile, pornographic photographs of Amy have been in circulation since the 1990s, the lawsuit says. Dubbed the “Misty” series, those images “consistently appear in collections maintained by individuals who possess child pornography,” the lawsuit says. And photos from that collection were “seized from Epstein’s properties.” But Amy was never notified, according to the lawsuit. And her lawyers contend that the only child porn Epstein victims who were contacted by the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children “were limited to a small number that were addressed in the Ghislaine Maxwell trial.” Nappi said: “We want the estate to preserve and account for everything seized from Epstein’s properties, and we want a real, court supervised process to identify and notify every survivor depicted in that collection. Many of them have no idea their images exist in his files, and they deserve to know, and they deserve the chance to seek justice.” NCMEC had no comment when it was asked whether it has identified and contacted any of the other women whose images were in Epstein’s possession. The private, nonprofit organization’s mission is to help find missing children and combat child sexual exploitation. Maxwell was convicted in December 2021 of recruiting and grooming teenage girls to be sexually abused by Epstein. She is serving a 20-year prison term for conspiring to sex traffic minors. And, according to a whistleblower report to Congress last year, she sought to get her sentence commuted by President Donald Trump. Trump, a once-close friend of Epstein’s who adamantly maintains he did not know Epstein was preying on young girls, has not granted Maxwell’s request.

articles.title: For checkpoint and settler attack news, Palestinians tune into the radio
articles.summary: Palestinians in the West Bank navigate Israeli road closures and attacks with help from a local radio station.
articles.body:
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank know they shouldn’t ask what time their loved ones are going to make it home.

There’s simply no way to give an accurate answer. What used to be a short ride from one place to another could now take hours, or it might not happen at all.

Before driving, Palestinians check dedicated WhatsApp and Telegram groups and channels where people share updates on road conditions. But this isn’t typical traffic news: Instead, chats focus on which Israeli military checkpoints are open, which roads are off limits to Palestinians and whether Israeli settlers are attacking Palestinians as they drive their vehicles.

Sometimes pins are sent to warn people driving near towns where Israeli forces are conducting raids.

And if there’s no time to check the groups, then there’s always Basma FM. The Palestinian radio station, based in Rawabi near Ramallah, carries three traffic updates per hour.

The channel started broadcasting on October 2, 2023 – just days before the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7 and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and what has become a pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank.

“Our idea was to target young people. We wanted to offer entertainment and culture news. But five days later, we realised we couldn’t,” said Fatima Barqawi, Basma FM’s news and traffic director.

The team had originally planned traffic updates as part of their programming. “We thought we could tell parents picking up their children from school to know where there was traffic, but after the war on Gaza started, we had to shift focus,” Barqawi said.

Her department has seven employees who verify information with their sources and provide updates on roadblocks.

“Things change each second. We could say there’s a closed checkpoint and Israeli soldiers decide to reopen it. Or vice versa,” Barqawi explained.

The issue for Palestinians driving through the West Bank isn’t simply being late for appointments or held up for hours – it’s that there is an inherent danger to travelling in the occupied territory.

Palestinians in the West Bank drive white-plated vehicles, making them easily identifiable compared to the yellow-plated cars driven by Israeli settlers.

Israeli soldiers have killed Palestinians near checkpoints after claiming they were conducting ramming attacks, and Israeli settlers often attack Palestinian cars or block them from using certain highways.

These attacks are increasing as illegal Israeli settlements grow at a record pace.

It is hard to miss the large infrastructure projects Israel is implementing, expanding highways to connect Israeli settlements to one another and to Israel. This ends up isolating Palestinian communities, often forcing Palestinians to use poorly paved roads or dangerous mountainous routes to avoid Israeli settlers and roadblocks.

It’s a journey of fear and anxiety, a young Palestinian woman who did not wish to be named told Al Jazeera. “I used to blast my music and drive, now I’m on high alert. Always on edge.”

The woman recounted how Israeli soldiers assaulted her fiancé near a checkpoint in Hebron, in the southern occupied West Bank, because they mistakenly thought he had passed without stopping. A year later, she said, a soldier pointed his rifle at her.

“He was shouting at me. The sun was blocking my view, and I was careful crossing the checkpoint but that wasn’t enough. I saw the green beam [from the gun] and thought that was the end,” she said.

Many Palestinians report being assaulted, humiliated and sometimes arrested at these checkpoints and roadblocks.

Israel has long imposed movement restrictions on Palestinians, controlling the road system and Palestinians’ access to the wider world. But since the war on Gaza began, these restrictions have intensified.

As of December 2025, the United Nations documented 925 barriers across the occupied West Bank including East Jerusalem, a 43 percent increase over the 20-year annual average of 647, the UN’s humanitarian affairs agency, OCHA, reported.

Almost all of of the villages and cities in the West Bank have iron gates at their entrances, and Israeli forces close them arbitrarily. Some of the gates are only open during certain hours.

A new report by the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem said the restrictions are used to deliberately fragment Palestinian life, with roadblocks and military checkpoints cutting off people from their work, schools, hospitals and one another.

The report, titled The Elimination Project, says there’s a broad rapid and systematic Israeli assault in the West Bank that aims to dismantle the foundations of Palestinian existence, and road closures are just one of them.

That is why, as Heba Erkat prepared her notes before heading into the studio for Basma FM’s Wednesday afternoon bulletin, she knew the information about to be read out could change rapidly.

Her colleague read the news, and then Erkat started listing updates at 61 checkpoints across the West Bank.

It was a relatively good day: only 12 of the checkpoints were either closed or had long queues.

But, as Erkat noted at the end of the segment, “the situation changes by the minute”.

articles.title: Electricity discount: £63 to be paid to NI households
articles.summary: The one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills will be paid from next month.
articles.body:
All households in Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from next month.

It is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market.

The schemes are being funded by the UK government and will be applied automatically without the need for an application.

Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter.

The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go.

That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up.

The Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise".

Last week applications opened for a separate means-tested scheme to provide a £100 voucher to some heating oil users. It is jointly funded by Stormont and the UK government.

The electricity scheme reflects two policies which apply in GB: a temporary cut in VAT and the removal tax of some consumer levies.

The UK government decided not to apply the VAT cut in NI as it would have required agreement with the EU which it thought would lead to delay.

It comes as energy prices continue to rise, driven by the US conflict with Iran.

Data from the NI consumer council suggests 500 litres of home heating oil currently costs around £560, more than twice the price compared to this time last year.

articles.title: Interest rates hold expected but Bank of England facing tough choices
articles.summary: Forecasts of further rises in the inflation rate mean some analysts expect the Bank to act by the end of the year.
articles.body:
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to keep interest rates unchanged despite price rises accelerating due to the prolonged conflict in the Middle East.

The nine-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has been meeting amid a backdrop of increasing global energy prices and interest rate rises around the world.

Economists expect the MPC to hold the benchmark Bank rate at 3.75% for a sixth consecutive meeting but analysts are more divided on whether the rate will need to go up before the end of the year.

The Bank rate is crucial in setting the benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest for individuals and businesses borrowing and saving money.

The latest interest rate decision will be announced by the Bank at 12:00 BST on Thursday.

Following its previous meeting at the end of July, the MPC indicated it could raise the Bank rate if the Iran war escalated.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey told the BBC at the time: "If we get a continuation of this conflict going on and oil prices stay above $100 a barrel... the odds are that interest rates will have to go up higher."

Oil prices moved above the $100 (£74) level on 9 September , and have remained there since, and there are few signs of a lasting truce in the Iran war.

The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%.

However, official figures released on Wednesday showed the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation had risen to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July , pushing it to its highest rate in six months.

The acceleration was driven by rises in the cost of petrol, diesel and airfares.

Economists expect that higher global energy costs will feed through to food and fuel prices paid by consumers, meaning the inflation rate is yet to peak.

The MPC will be aware that, citing the Middle East conflict and warning inflation was "set to remain well above" its 2% target for some time, the European Central Bank recently raised interest rates to 2.5%.

In addition, the US Federal Reserve raised its interest rate to 3.5%-3.75% for similar reasons on Wednesday.

However, MPC members will also be keen not to put pressure on employers and further lower the prospects for those seeking a job.

Households feel the impact of a rising Bank rate through higher borrowing costs, but can benefit from more generous savings rates.

Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages in recent days.

Andrew Montlake, chief executive of mortgage broker Coreco, said that the latest data showed that "the inflation dragon has not been fully slain".

"If inflation proves sticky, lenders' funding costs stay under pressure, which makes cheaper mortgages harder to deliver," he said.

"We are already seeing lenders reprice upwards, so this will do little to calm things down. Borrowers should not panic, but anyone approaching the end of a fixed rate should start looking early, secure an option and keep reviewing it."

The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

Savers may be offered more generous returns, but the spending power of their savings could be eroded by the rising cost of living.

"It's almost impossible to time things just right, so I would urge households to focus on what's best for them now, in the medium term and in the longer term," said Harriet Guevara, chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society.

"For savers, regularly check that your savings are earning a competitive return and that you have the right balance between easy access and money you can afford to put away for longer."

articles.title: Young newlyweds killed after boat collides with water taxi and sinks in Venice lagoon
articles.summary: Two young newlyweds were collecting bait near Burano when their boat collided with a five-ton water taxi in the Venetian Lagoon. They both died; an investigation has begun.
articles.body: A pair of young newlyweds were killed in an accident involving a water taxi in Venice just three months after they were married. Gabriella Querino, 26, and Sean Michieli, 25, were killed Saturday morning in a collision involving a 5-ton water taxi, Jam Press reported. The couple was in a boat that had departed from Burano, an island in the Venetian Lagoon, about 6 miles northeast of central Venice. Querino was reported missing in the immediate aftermath of the crash, and search efforts were hampered by strong currents and poor visibility. Her body was eventually recovered from the lagoon. Michieli was rushed to Venice-Mestre Hospital with severe head and facial injuries and other injuries across his body. He was pronounced brain-dead the next day. CRUISES THROWN INTO CHAOS AS DROUGHT STRANDS SHIPS, LEAVES PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING Querino, originally from Ribeirão Preto, Brazil, moved to Italy about two years ago. She developed a passion for fishing alongside her husband, who was from Cavallino-Treporti, Italy, according to Jam Press. articles.title: Aggrieved party can seek deletion of court clips on socials: SC
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In an important clarification on the ban on use of video clips of court proceedings, Supreme Court on Wednesday said if such footage was up.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In an important clarification on the ban on use of video clips of court proceedings, Supreme Court on Wednesday said if such footage was uploaded on social media, an aggrieved person could approach the authorities under the Information and Technology Act to seek a "takedown" order of the content.This clarification came from a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while hearing a petition filed by an advocate whose arguments on July 1 before one of the SC benches on behalf of his father, accused of jumping bail, went viral on social media.Counsel for the advocate said unauthorised circulation of the proceedings on social media platforms had violated his right to life, liberty, dignity and privacy. "Continuous availability of the impugned videos on social media platforms, even after express judicial orders prohibiting such dissemination, constitutes an ongoing and irreparable injury to the petitioner's fundamental rights," he said.The bench said the SC had passed the ban order on July 24, and the lawyer could approach authorities under the IT Act and seek takedown orders against digital and social media platforms for deleting the alleged offensive content being circulated despite a ban imposed by the top court.CJI Kant said there was an efficacious remedy available to the advocate and he must avail that. However, he clarified that if any social media or digital platform used footage from livestreaming of court proceedings and either added a narrative or exhibited clips selectively to convey a different meaning, it would be viewed very seriously and may amount to contempt of court."If someone adds something to what the court observed or presents the proceedings in such a manner to generate controversy, we will take a very serious view of such acts," the CJI said.The bench advised the lawyer to move the authorities under Section 69A of the IT Act or directly send a legal notice to digital and social media platforms to take down the offensive content. If the intermediaries or authorities did not respond to the request and the grievance remained unresolved, he could file a petition in the SC, it said.Frowning upon edited clips of live-streamed judicial proceedings accompanied by biased commentary flooding social media, the SC on July 24 had banned uploading, sharing and circulation of audiovisual excerpts of court hearings on social media and digital platforms and said any online posting of such clips would require mandatory prior approval from the SC or jurisdictional HCs.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: New hope for breast cancer patients as life-extending drug now on NHS in England
articles.summary: Enhertu, which can give patients an extra seven months to live on average, has been prescribed in Scotland for more than two years and is available.
articles.body:
Patients in England with a specific type of incurable breast cancer can now access a life-extending drug on the NHS, two years after it was deemed too expensive by a health body.

Enhertu can give patients almost seven extra months to live on average - with some living up to three years longer.

Women in Scotland have had access to the drug on the NHS since 2023, and it is available in 26 other European countries.

Charities and patients have campaigned for it to be more widely available since 2024, when the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) said Enhertu was not good value for money.

From Thursday, doctors in England are now able to prescribe it, with Wales expected to follow shortly but the guidance doesn't automatically apply to Northern Ireland.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "Enhertu can be life-changing, and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it.

"It is a tribute to the campaigners and charities who never stopped pressing for this."

This decision will affect about 1,000 women a year with a specific type of breast cancer, HER2-low.

Charity Breast Cancer Now said that while campaigners' "persistence paid off", thousands of people have missed out on access to Enhertu and many have died.

The charity's chief executive, Claire Rowney, said: "Today we can finally say we did it." However, she adds that "we can't celebrate this momentous decision without remembering the devastating cost of this delay".

Kate Wills, 51, understands this mix of emotions. She has HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, which has spread to her bones and lungs. But nothing about her suggests that she is terminally ill.

She has a high-powered job and is a wife and mum. Her social media feed shows a full and happy life - only the occasional medical appointment hints all is not well.

Kate says it has been "incredibly painful" to know that Enhertu could keep her alive for longer but she couldn't get it.

When she hears it will be available on the NHS, she immediately starts crying. "I really can't believe it. I'm so relieved, I'm overjoyed," she says.

"It's so hard keeping hope when you have stage four cancer. This gives me enormous hope."

Her son and daughter are in their teens and early 20s. Kate has been aiming to stay alive long enough for her youngest to finish school.

She smiles through her tears as she says: "Now I've just dared to dream that I might be around to see them fall in love, to get married."

For her, this is bittersweet. Her first thought is for "those women, my friends, who didn't get this in time".

One of those was Jeannie Ambrose, who was full of life and fight when she spoke to BBC News two years ago aged 53.

She told us: "I'm not ready to die yet. I want to stay alive, I want to keep living. I should be concentrating on enjoying time with my family and friends. I should not be campaigning, using the time I've got left to fight."

Jeannie died in January this year. Kate says her friend would would be "thrilled but also angry at how long it's taken and how rejected we've felt".

The BBC understands that the drug companies Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca have not substantially lowered their prices since the drug was first rejected.

The reason NICE has reversed its decision is largely because of a trade deal with the USA, where the UK government agreed to spend 25% more on medicines.

As part of this, NICE has increased how much the NHS will pay for every extra year of good quality life a medication can give.

This is known as a QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) - and the upper threshold per QALY has gone from £30,000 to £35,000.

At the end of August, NICE also introduced a different, more nuanced, way of measuring a patient's quality of life.

These two changes were enough to tip the balance.

It is thought that patient campaigns for Enhertu - and other drugs - have helped too.

Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca welcome NICE's decision, but the latter is calling for "strong collaboration" across the healthcare system to ensure "faster, more equitable patient access in the future".

Breast Cancer Now's Claire Rowney says: "We are calling on the government, NICE, NHS England and the pharmaceutical industry to work together to fix this broken system, so that people with incurable metastatic breast cancer are not forced to spend precious months and years campaigning for treatments that could give them more time."

Helen Knight, director of medicines evaluation at NICE, says she is pleased a "commercial solution" means the treatment can be made available on the NHS in England but adds she knows the decision "comes too late for many families".

"Our role is important in ensuring NHS spending on new medicines reflects the benefits they deliver while protecting valuable health resources for other essential patient services," she says.

For Kate, the thought of dying before she had to, "when there was a drug that I just could almost reach but couldn't get", was "so incredibly painful".

"To know that I can get it now is absolutely everything."

articles.title: "They convinced Erika to get behind it": Candace Owens makes new claim about Charlie Kirk family’s wrongful death lawsuit as legal battle takes shape
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Candace Owens has reignited questions surrounding the wrongful death case linked to Charlie Kirk’s death, claiming that the lawsuit was driven by Kirk.
articles.body: Candace Owens has reignited questions surrounding the wrongful death case linked to Charlie Kirk’s death, claiming that the lawsuit was driven by Kirk’s parents rather than Turning Point USA or his widow, Erika Kirk. Her post comes as Kirk’s family takes formal legal steps against Utah Valley University and the state of Utah, alleging that security failures at the campus contributed to his fatal shooting in September 2025.Candace Owens claims Charlie Kirk’s parents pushed the lawsuitOwens addressed the issue in a post on September 16, where she directly disputed what she described as attempts by Turning Point USA to take credit for the legal action.She wrote:“Since there is nothing that TPUSA won’t try to grift off of, I feel it’s important to state something that is true:The wrongful death lawsuit was pushed by Charlie Kirk’s parents. They were the ones that wanted this justice for Charlie and they approached and convinced Erika to get behind it.This is a fact.”Owens presented the statement as a factual correction, but her account should be understood as her claim about how the lawsuit came together. The post does not itself provide documents establishing that sequence of events.The legal filing itself confirms that Kirk’s family is pursuing claims connected to his death. A September 9 notice of claim notified Utah Valley University and the state of Utah of the family’s intention to seek damages. The filing names Kirk’s estate and heirs, including Erika Kirk and their two children, while his parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, are also listed among the prospective plaintiffs.Charlie Kirk family lawsuit focuses on alleged security failuresThe legal action centres on what Kirk’s family says happened before and during the September 10, 2025, event at Utah Valley University.According to the notice, Turning Point USA had raised concerns about access to rooftops overlooking the area where Kirk was scheduled to speak. The family alleges that university police were warned about the potential security problem, but the rooftop from which Kirk was shot was not adequately secured.One exchange cited in the legal documents has drawn particular attention. After a Turning Point USA staff member raised concerns about rooftop access, UVU Police Chief Jeffrey Long allegedly responded, "I got you covered." The family argues that the university nevertheless failed to prevent access to the rooftop used by the shooter.The notice also alleges inadequate event planning, including insufficient police staffing and a lack of measures to monitor nearby rooftops. The family further argues that emergency response arrangements were inadequate, with Kirk ultimately being transported to a hospital in a private vehicle rather than an ambulance. These are allegations contained in the family's legal notice, not findings established by a court.Utah Valley University has acknowledged receiving the notice and said it would address the matter through its established legal processes. The Utah attorney general's office has not commented on the potential litigation.Meanwhile, Tyler Robinson, who is accused of killing Kirk, has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty, and the criminal case is moving toward trial.Owens' comments therefore add another layer to an already closely watched legal fight, placing renewed attention on the role Kirk's parents, Erika Kirk and Turning Point USA may have played in bringing the wrongful death action forward.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hospitals could be charging you 2,841% higher on commonly used consumables
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: An IV infusion set priced in the wholesale market for Rs 11 carries an MRP of Rs 325, while a disposable syringe available for under Rs 7 h.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An IV infusion set priced in the wholesale market for Rs 11 carries an MRP of Rs 325, while a disposable syringe available for under Rs 7 has a price tag of around Rs 60, putting a spotlight on one of the least visible components of hospital bills: the price of widely used consumables during treatment. The gap becomes even more stark for high-value devices such as pacemakers, heart valves and intraocular lenses, where the final MRP may be 10-30 fold higher than the import landed price.Such huge mark-ups ultimately inflate the patient's hospital bill and may add significantly to the out-of-pocket treatment cost.The issue has been flagged multiple times over last 15 years but a fresh push by Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has revived a question that has remained unresolved for years: who ultimately sets price of a medical device - the manufacturer, the hospital or the regulator?Several earlier analyses by National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) of hospital bills had shown how certain private hospitals procured consumables at rock-bottom prices but charged patients the high printed MRP, sources told TOI.Flagging mark-ups as high as 2,841% on commonly used hospital consumables, Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra FDA commissioner, posted on X on Tuesday, "The regulatory gap is structural: scheduled medicines are capped under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. Most medical devices and consumables are not, leaving both the pricing and the information around it almost entirely unmonitored.'' He urged the Centre to frame guidelines to address the "permissible gap between trade procurement price and declared MRP".Nearly a decade ago, prices for cardiac stents and orthopaedic knee implants were capped by NPPA. And, in 2020, govt capped trade margins on certain critical items, including pulse oximeters, blood pressure monitors and glucometers, during the Coronavirus pandemic.Historically, the industry - domestic and MNCs - have been split over the capping of trade margins. The domestic industry represented by AiMeD cautioned that the current regulatory framework under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, is inadequate to address the pricing of medical devices and has proposed capping trade margins at 75% for widely used consumables such as syringes and IV sets, and at 50% for high-value devices such as pacemakers and heart valves."Genuine device manufacturers and importers are at a clear disadvantage under the current system of unchecked hospital mark-ups. Ethical suppliers price their products transparently, based on ex-factory or landed import price, but when hospitals inflate MRPs by 10-30 times, the market rewards those willing to play the distortion game. Responsible companies that refuse to indulge in excessive margins are forced out of competition or in order to survive, have to comply with these unfair demands,'' said Rajiv Nath, forum coordinator, AiMeD, saidAs against this, Medical Technology Association of India, which represents MNCs, said it concurred with Maharashtra FDA Commissioner's "three asks of margin rationalisation, an inter-agency review and clear guidelines governing the permissible gap between trade procurement costs and declared MRPs", which is the "essence of Trade Margin Rationalisation".Get the latest India News and Live updates.
